# Hoshin Kanri — X-Matrix

Connect long-term breakthrough objectives to this year's targets, the strategies that will move them, and the metrics that prove it — with a specificity check that pushes back on vague plans instead of formatting them.

Family: Hoshin Kanri · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

Hoshin Kanri ("direction management") is how an organisation turns a long-term direction into this year's work, without the connection between the two getting lost. The X-Matrix is its signature artifact: one page linking long-term breakthrough objectives, this year's annual objectives, the improvement strategies that will move them, and the metrics that prove it — with a correlation grid at each intersection showing exactly how strong each connection actually is. Catchball is the negotiation that gets you there: objectives don't arrive fully formed from the top, they're proposed, pushed back on, and refined at every level before they're locked in.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- You have real organisational authority to set direction — you can commit resources and hold people accountable to the objectives that come out of this.
- There's a genuine long-term direction to connect this year's work to, not just a list of projects looking for a rationale.
- You're willing to have the plan pushed back on. A Hoshin plan padded with vague aspirations is worse than no plan — it creates the feeling of direction without the substance.

Not when:

- You're an individual contributor without the authority to commit a team's resources — Hoshin cascades through an organisation; nobody runs it alone the way one person can run a 5-Whys. Use an A3 for a bounded problem you can actually act on yourself.
- The "long-term objectives" are really just this year's project list relabelled — there's no real 3-5 year direction underneath them.
- You want to skip catchball and go straight to a finished matrix. A matrix nobody negotiated is a document, not a plan — it won't survive contact with the first budget conversation.

## How to fill it in

- **trueNorth** — One or two sentences: why does this plan exist? Every objective on the page should trace back to this. If you can't draw that line for an objective, it doesn't belong on this plan.
- **longTermObjectives** — Where does the organisation need to be in three to five years? Give each one a target that's unambiguous when reached — "be more competitive" isn't checkable; "grow market share from 12% to 20%" is.
- **annualObjectives** — What has to be true by the end of this year to be on track for the long-term objectives? These are what actually get worked this year — the long-term objectives set direction, the annual objectives set the pace.
- **catchball** — The record of who proposed each annual objective, how another level pushed back, and what was actually agreed. This isn't paperwork — an objective that was never negotiated with the people who have to deliver it is a wish, not a commitment.
- **strategies** — The improvement initiatives that will actually move the annual objectives. Name an owner for each — a strategy with no owner doesn't happen, it just sits on the page looking like progress.
- **metrics** — What you'll track to know the strategies are working, each with a target. If a strategy has no metric watching it, you'll find out it failed only when the year is over.
- **correlations** — The heart of the X-Matrix: which long-term objectives each annual objective actually supports, which metrics track each objective, which strategies move each metric, and which strategies support which long-term objectives. Mark primary, secondary, or weak — and leave a pair blank when there's genuinely no connection. A matrix where everything correlates with everything isn't rigorous, it's decoration.

## What good looks like

The example below is a full X-Matrix: long-term objectives and annual objectives with real targets, a catchball record showing the negotiation behind them, strategies with named owners, metrics with targets, and a correlation grid that's honest about which connections are strong and which are weak — not a fully-shaded matrix pretending everything connects to everything.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://www.katafacts.com/katas/hoshin-kanri

## Common mistakes

- **Objectives read like a mission statement, not a target.** — "Be a leader in customer experience" can't be checked. If two people could reasonably disagree about whether it was achieved, it isn't specific enough to plan against yet.
- **The correlation matrix is fully shaded — everything connects to everything.** — A matrix that looks that dense usually means the correlations weren't actually thought through. The useful information in an X-Matrix is which connections are weak or absent, not just which are present.
- **Catchball is skipped and the matrix goes straight from an executive offsite to a finished document.** — The people asked to deliver the strategies never got a chance to push back on feasibility. The plan looks complete and isn't tested.
- **A strategy has no owner, or a metric has no target.** — This is exactly what the specificity check exists to catch — an unowned strategy or untargeted metric is a line on a page, not a commitment.
- **One person builds the whole X-Matrix alone to save time.** — Hoshin's value comes from the organisation aligning around the plan, not from the document itself. A matrix nobody else was involved in building has no more authority than an opinion.

## What it connects to

Downstream:

- **A3 problem solving** — When a strategy on the X-Matrix isn't moving its metric, an A3 is the right tool to find out why and close the gap — Hoshin sets the direction, A3 closes the specific gaps along the way.
- **Value stream mapping** — A strategy aimed at a process (not a single problem) often starts with a value stream map of the current state before committing to what the strategy actually is.
- **Performance board** — This is the bowler chart: tracks the metrics named here over time, cadence by cadence, computed red or green from real numbers — the X-Matrix sets what to watch; a performance board is where you watch it. A ready-to-fill static template is also available in the resource library if you'd rather start from a blank workbook.
- **Cascade map** — Shows how this X-Matrix's annual objectives become the long-term objectives of the level below it — the mechanism that makes Hoshin cascade through an organisation rather than living at one level.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Committing to the actual objectives, targets, and owners
- Deciding what a catchball response actually resolves to
- Judging whether a strategy is really worth the resources it would take

Analysis — AI helps:

- Challenging vague objectives, strategies, and metrics that sound specific but aren't checkable
- Proposing a first-pass correlation matrix from the stated objectives, strategies, and metrics for the practitioner to correct
- Flagging an objective that doesn't actually trace back to the stated true north

Drudgery — automated:

- Formatting the X-Matrix — rotated axis labels, correlation symbols at the right intersections, merged cells
- Keeping the correlation grid's row/column references in sync as objectives and strategies are edited
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
